fields.country: multi-country (Bangladesh: Dhaka and Chittagong; India: Hyderabad; Kenya: Nairobi)
fields.subnational_unit: ten slum and squatter settlements (two each in Dhaka and Chittagong, three each in Hyderabad and Nairobi) and several pavement-dweller locations
fields.sample_size: Three-year qualitative ethnographic study (2003-2005, DFID-funded): ten slum and squatter settlements of varying tenure security in Chittagong, Dhaka, Hyderabad and Nairobi plus several pavement locations; case-study households and individuals were followed intensively for three to six months each, with local officials and NGOs consulted; the number of households or interviews is not stated (the authors say a headcount was not the aim); one subsample of 33 homeless (street and pavement) respondents is cited
fields.effect_measure: qualitative ethnographic findings; no quantitative estimate
fields.effect_estimate: Official recognition and tenure, not need, decided who got sanitation. In Nairobi, where all slums are officially illegal, 70 per cent of the residents of Maili Saba (settled since the 1930s) had never had any public or donor-provided service while Kibera drew many uncoordinated agencies; in Dhaka the unrecognised Mazar Road settlement, which no agency served, was bulldozed with one day's notice two weeks into the fieldwork; slums become 'notified' or 'adopted' by chance and political leverage rather than by length of settlement or need; homeless pavement dwellers were reached by no water or sanitation programme. What was provided (low-cost household excreta disposal and handwashing messages) did not fit gendered and spatial needs: a 14-seater UNICEF community latrine in the 'illegal' Beguntila settlement (Dhaka), used by about 1,500 people daily, was near-dysfunctional four years after construction (broken doors, no water or lights, full septic tank). The authors conclude that the mismatch, not lack of demand, explains non-use and non-sustainability, and that until the technical, financial and ethical discrepancies are resolved there is little reason to celebrate the recent global declaration of the human right to water and sanitation.
fields.legal_status: notified or adopted slums versus unrecognised or illegal settlements and homeless pavement dwellers
fields.section: Full text (journal article, 21 pages): I. Sanitation for the urban poor; II. Rethinking gender, sanitation and urban poverty (study design); III. Who are the urban poor?; IV. Appropriate sanitation: experiences and perceptions; V. Appropriate for whom? What is provided versus what is required
fields.exact_location: Section II (study design, pp. 92-94); section III (settlement recognition, tenure and eviction: Mazar Road, Maili Saba, Kibera); section V (Beguntila community latrine)
fields.risk_of_bias_rating: CASP Qualitative per-item (re-appraised 2026-10-09 on the full text; supersedes the abstract-only rating): 1(aims)=Yes; 2(qual approach)=Yes; 3(design)=Yes (multi-site ethnography; settlements chosen to vary in tenure security, with the unplanned selection of Mazar Road explained); 4(recruitment)=Can't tell (case-study households were chosen to include the most vulnerable, but their number and the selection procedure are not given, and the initial settlements were those where agencies already worked); 5(data collection)=Yes (three to six months of ethnography per household, day and night visits, regular dialogue with local policy professionals); 6(researcher-participant)=Yes (the paper discusses participants' fatigue with researchers, their hopes of aid and the resulting conflicts); 7(ethics)=Can't tell (no ethics or consent statement located); 8(analysis rigor)=Can't tell (no analysis method described; the authors accept that the stories may be called anecdotal); 9(findings)=Yes; 10(value)=Yes. Per CASP's own guidance no composite score is computed.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a three-year qualitative ethnographic study (2003-2005) of ten slum and squatter settlements and pavement locations in Chittagong, Dhaka, Hyderabad and Nairobi; legal recognition and tenure security determined who received sanitation; no quantitative estimate; read in full text 2026-10-09.
